body.p: Index style Index format Editors and authors are sometimes not sure where responsibilities lie when it comes to formatting the index. The answer is really pretty simple: Whoever is responsible for the layout, composition, and formatting of the book as a whole also needs to be responsible for formatting the index.

section.title: What to Expect When the Index Arrives: Style
section.p: When an index arrives from the indexer, the editor can expect certain aspects of the index to already be in place. These include the choice of style (run-in or indented), capitalization, and punctuation.

Run-in style Indented style Entriesrun-in vs. indented The two most common index styles are run-in and indented. In run-in style, subheadings follow the main heading on the same line, separated by semicolons. In indented style, each subheading begins on a new line with an indent.

Spelling conventions Punctuation in indexes Spelling and punctuation should follow the conventions established by the style guide in use. Common style guides include the Chicago Manual of Style and Hart’s Rules.

section.title: Capitalization
section.p: Capitalization Conventions for capitalization in indexes vary. Some house styles require capitalizing the first word of every main heading, while others use lowercase throughout except for proper nouns. The important thing is consistency.

section.title: Cross-Reference Style
section.p: Cross-referencesstyle of Cross-references should be formatted according to house style. See and See also are commonly italicized, and the referenced heading may be capitalized or not depending on the convention used.

section.title: Abbreviation of Page Ranges
section.p: Abbreviation of page ranges Page ranges Conflation of page numbers Chicago Manual of Style (University of Chicago Press)Chicago Manual of Style Page ranges may be expressed in full (132–138) or abbreviated (132–38 or 132–8). The Chicago Manual of Style provides detailed guidance on acceptable abbreviation patterns. Conflation of page numbers (combining two references into a single range) should be done carefully to avoid misrepresentation.

section.title: Diacriticals and Special Characters
section.p: Accent marks (diacriticals) Accent marks and other diacritical characters should be preserved in index entries. This is particularly important for personal and place names from non-English languages.

section.title: Illustrative Material
section.p: Art books Illustrative material in indexes References to figures, tables, maps, and other illustrative material are typically indicated by special typography (such as italics or bold) in the index locators. Art books may require specialized indexing approaches.

section.title: Index Evaluation Checklist
section.p: Checklist for index evaluation Communicationimportance of A comprehensive evaluation checklist helps editors verify that the index meets quality standards. Communication between editor and indexer about style expectations before the indexing begins can prevent many problems.
